title: Nanoscale Near Field Imaging of Surface Plasmons by Ultrafast Electron Microscopy
content: Surface plasmon resonance is collective oscillation of surface charge around metal nanostructures or at the interface between a metal and a dielectric material. Surface plasmons resonance has been widely used in biological sensing, Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS), waveguiding, photovoltaics, photocatalysis, ultrafast communication, and quantum computing due to strong optical absorption, scattering and electromagnetic field confinement beyond the diffraction limit. [1,2] The localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPR) energies are highly sensitive to the shape, size, and composition of the plasmonic materials and the surrounding dielectric environments.[3] The surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) propagate along the interface and exhibits exponential decays perpendicular to the interface into an adjacent dielectric medium. With the unique properties of evanescence and surface localization, SPPs are non-radiative and can be transversely localized and guided into subwavelength metallic structures as small as a few nanometers.[4] The SPPs depend on surface roughness, interface optical properties, propagation distance, excitation wavelength. Therefore, it is of great importance to image the surface plasmons at the nanometer scale to gain deeper understanding of the propagation and localization of light below the diffraction limit for exploring its applications.
